newsitem.title: UK: IPE shops for OPEC business, welcomes Labour reform.
newsitem.headline: IPE shops for OPEC business, welcomes Labour reform.

text.p: Middle East oil producers are being targeted by the International Petroleum Exchange in its efforts to boost volume after a "credibility" problem with its gas oil contract scared away some physical traders last winter, IPE Chief Executive Lynton Jones said in an interview.

Jones said he met Kuwaiti energy and investment officials at a recent conference in Abu Dhabi and that individuals in the Middle East involved in the oil industry have accepted offers to attend IPE seminars on hedging and using the futures markets.
The Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), now comprising 11 member states, has in the past been wary of trading in volatile futures markets.
"There is of course a reluctance on the part of Moslem countries to use futures markets for ideological reasons," Jones said.
"Nevertheless it seems to me pretty clear that some of the investment authorities, whether directly or indirectly, are becoming users of our market place and the other energy markets."

"We don't think there is anything to be gained in trying to push these countries into this market place faster than they would be comfortable but I think that in the long term they will certainly become users of the market," he said.

The exchange's goal was to globalise its contracts and align itself more closely with the physical market, and "see whether we could bring in participants who are not currently using the markets, for example the Middle East and India," he added.
Talks with the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) on a 24-hour joint trading system are also advancing and should lead to an agreement by their summer deadline, he said.

IPE officials will meet with their NYMEX counterparts in New York on May 12 and talks hopefully will widen to eventually include the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX), a key player in the link up, he said.

"On the basis of the discussions we've had so far there is reason to hope that we can achieve something within that time scope, but a lot of it depends upon factors over which we don't have direct control," Jones said.

An agreement between IPE and SIMEX, the second and third largest oil markets respectively, gives the Singapore exchange trading rights over the flagship Brent crude futures contract during Far East hours.

Closer to home, Labour's victory in the British election last Thursday was welcomed by Jones as long as reform in the financial services industry leads to a reduction in the cost of regulation, a chunk of the exchange's costs.
Labour said before the election it would merge existing regulatory bodies with top financial watchdog the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) if elected.
"My feeling is that if it reduces the cost of regulation it is to be welcomed. If it increases the efficiency of regulation it is to be welcomed," Jones said.
In meetings with the exchange, Labour also indicated it would continue much of the deregulation in the energy industry outlined by the Conservatives, he added.

Jones, a former member of the British foreign service, admitted to needing his diplomatic skills in his first year on the job. Trading volume on the IPE was flat, its gas oil contract suffered during the critical winter heating season and commission rates squeezed profits of brokers on the floor of the exchange.

Proposals will be presented to the IPE's board on May 19 on ways to improve its gas oil contract after an independent review criticised the exchange for failing to enforce its own rules and not standing up for its biggest customers, the large oil trading companies.

"I think that the majority of the recommendations... (of the review) made were probably acceptable to the majority of the people in the market place," Jones said, noting the most contentious was position limits.
Some big players may stay away from gas oil after the recommendations are implemented but the long-term credibility of the contract would be renewed, he said.
"Clearly what we need to do is re-establish the credibility of the contract to make sure that it is tightly in line with the physical marketplace," he said.

He also warned that more brokers may withdraw from the market because of falling commissions. Just last week, trading sources said Salomon Inc's subsidiary PhiBro halved its IPE trading team to six from 12.

"It is possible we will see sooner or later other players withdrawing from the market because there is simply not enough orders out there from end users to justify the number of people who are broking the business," he said.

The infant natural gas contract has been one hope, but the IPE is considering changing the size of the contract's minimum price movement and the electronic display of prices to boost its volume, he said.
Natural gas open interest has grown and the end-users have responded favourably to the contract, while low volume can be blamed on a quiet physical market, he said.

The exchange is still considering whether to stay put or move within the financial City district or to the Docklands, he said. A consultant hired by the IPE will present its findings to the board in June or July.
